questions.q: Name the two terminals of an electric cell.
questions.a: Positive terminal (metal cap) and negative terminal (metal disc).

questions.q: Where does current flow from and to in a cell?
questions.a: Conventionally from the positive terminal through the circuit back to the negative terminal.

questions.q: Why does a cell stop working after long use?
questions.a: The chemicals inside get used up and can no longer push current.

questions.q: Name the parts of an electric bulb.
questions.a: Glass bulb, thin filament, and two terminals (metal case at the side and metal tip at the base).

questions.q: What is the filament of a bulb?
questions.a: A very thin wire (usually of tungsten) that glows when current passes through it.
The filament burns out (breaks) after long use or too much current, stopping the circuit.
The complete path from one terminal of a cell through wires and a bulb back to the other terminal.

questions.q: When does the bulb in a circuit glow?
questions.a: When the circuit is closed (complete) - current flows through the filament.

questions.q: What happens when the circuit breaks anywhere?
questions.a: Current stops and the bulb goes off - an open circuit.
A device that opens (stops current) or closes (allows current) a circuit conveniently.

questions.q: Give two examples of switches at home.
questions.a: Light switches on walls and the push button of a torch.
It turns devices on and off safely without disconnecting wires.

questions.q: What are conductors and insulators of electricity?
questions.a: Conductors let current pass (metals, graphite); insulators block it (plastic, rubber, wood).

questions.q: Name the material used for electric wires and its cover.
Why should we never touch a switch with wet hands?
questions.a: Water (with dissolved salts) conducts; current can pass through the wet skin and shock us.
